newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS-Russia's last oil gem to be sold off.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Russia's last oil gem to be sold off.

text.p: Russia will bring the mass privatisation of its oil industry to a close this year by selling Rosneft for up to $1 billion.

Rosneft, once seen as an ugly duckling after its assets were hived off under sweeping restructuring of the world's third largest oil-producer, may yet turn into a swan for investors, some energy analysts said on Tuesday.

"It's an attractive company," said Elena Merkoulova, oil analyst at Salomon Brothers in London, citing Rosneft's large, strategically-located oil reserves in the Russian Far East. "But when it comes to the market, it will be a restructuring story."
Rosneft's total oil reserves, according to Russian standards, which tend to overstate size and commercial recoverability, are 10.82 billion barrels, or around 11.1 percent of the country's total.
The sell-off plan comes after senior Rosneft officials appear to have reached at least for now a consensus over what kind of future Rosneft should have.

Alexander Belov, first deputy head of Rosneft's privatisation and securities department, said on Tuesday Russia was likely to sell off 97 percent of Rosneft, including a 51 percent stake for hard cash in September.
He said the plan was approved by Energy Minister Boris Nemtsov and privatisation tsar Alfred Kokh, both of whom are under pressure to raise cash for the budget.

Employees and managers would receive up to three percent of the company, Belov said, while the rest would be offered through an investment tender, which requires winning bidders to promise to invest large sums.

"The sales could bring in $1 billion," Belov said, adding Rosneft would be sold with the Purneftegaz production unit, a key asset the ownership of which the courts have batted to and fro four times between Rosneft and rival oil group SIDANKO.

The sell-off plan may end a bitter debate between Rosneft's new president, Yuri Bespalov, and its board chairman and old president, Alexander Putilov -- men who, according to their minders, cannot bear to be in the same room at the same time.

And in what could signal a striking reversal both in Moscow's attitude to foreign investment and its need for money, Belov said Putilov might seek Kremlin approval to scrap a law limiting foreign ownership in oil companies to 15 percent.

Under the investment tender, the winner would be required to pay off Rosneft's tax arrears. Lia Levenson of Brunswick Brokerage said total tax arrears at the end of 1996 at Purneftegaz were $152 million equivalent, while at the Sakhalinmorneftegaz unit, they were $128 million.
Rosneft is already creating a scrum among Russian financiers and oil producers looking to add to their portfolios and loathe to miss the last vertically-integrated oil company up for grabs.

Boris Berezovsky, whose empire includes the Sibneft oil mini-major, is one interested party, Belov confirmed. Vladimir Potanin, president of powerful bank Uneximbank, which controls SIDANKO, and Russia's biggest oil company LUKoil are also keen.

Rosneft is unique among its Russian sisters in that it represents the state's interest in about $40 billion worth of production-sharing deals with foreign investors. It also has a 7.5 percent stake in a planned $2 billion oil pipeline to be built from Kazakhstan to Novorossiisk, Russia's oil export outlet on the Black Sea, and a large distribution system.

It has 38 percent in Purneftegaz and Sakhalinmorneftegaz, the latter a key oil producer in Russia's Far Eastern island Sakhalin, which is the locus of four major production-sharing projects with Western and Japanese oil majors.
But Rosneft also has drawbacks, like cost-intensive research institutes and struggling oil equipment producers.

One Western energy analyst said Rosneft's assets could still be stripped, adding that the decree making the firm the state's lifting agent could easily be reversed, while the procedure awarding reserves licences was done by fiat and was unclear.
